rule_name: an upstream name inside a registered re-implementation is accounted for
pattern: A step re-implements an upstream flow's configuration contract and reads a SUBSET of the variables that contract declares. Nothing anywhere records which subset. The step then refuses a declared thing as absent, because the declaration lives in a view reached only through one of the variables it never read, and the refusal is indistinguishable from a real absence: it names a count of the files it did open, it is worded correctly, and it is wrong. The omission is invisible from both sides -- our artefact never lists what we left out, and upstream has no idea anyone is mirroring it.
docstring: Where this plugin re-implements an upstream flow, every variable that flow declares must fall in exactly one recorded class: implemented, declared-unperformed, omitted with a reason, or a known gap with a reference. A name in no class is a finding the day it appears. This does not decide that the register is complete -- a re-implementation nobody registered is invisible to any program, and that judgement is a reader's. It removes the other failure, the one that actually happened, where the upstream was known, the re-implementation was known, and still no artefact said which parts of the contract had been left out.
fix_action: SHIPPED in this bundle. A register names each re-implementation, its upstream file, the extraction that yields the upstream declaration, a snapshot of that declaration with the content hash of the file it was read from, and our classification of every name in it. The check enforces classification completeness in BOTH directions, cross-checks every implemented name against our own module source so the register cannot claim an implementation the code does not contain, refuses a known gap that carries no reference, and refuses a known gap the module now implements so a closed gap cannot linger in the count of what is still wrong. Given a distribution root it re-measures the snapshot, reporting a name upstream has gained, a name upstream has dropped, and a content hash that no longer matches. An unreadable register, an entry with no upstream names, or an unreachable distribution is NOT DETERMINED, never a pass. Denominator printed at every verdict. Runs clean on this tree.

rule_name: a re-implemented computation names its pin or names its gap
pattern: A deterministic re-implementation of an upstream computation drifts from it. Upstream reads one dimension of a cell in both places it measures a side; ours read whichever dimension the oriented footprint presented, so one pair of sides summed the other dimension and over-counted by more than a factor of four. Nothing in the repository compared the two. The divergence produced no failure of its own -- it surfaced much later as a refusal about something else entirely, on a brief that was not about it, and every test of the module passed throughout because every test was written against the module's own arithmetic.
docstring: A registered re-implementation of an upstream computation must name either a pin test that compares ours against theirs, or a known gap with a reference. The upstream side is anchored by the STRING it is recognised by, not by a line number: a line number points ten lines above its subject after the next edit and still looks precise. When the anchor stops occurring in the upstream file, the computation we mirror has moved and the entry points at nothing, which is a finding. The check verifies the pin EXISTS and never that it is a good test -- that distinction is stated where a reader meets it, because a check that quietly implied more would be the same defect one layer up.
fix_action: SHIPPED in this bundle, as the second entry kind of the same register. A computation entry names our module, the upstream file, the anchor strings the computation is recognised by, a content hash of the upstream file at the moment it was read, and either a pin test as file-plus-function -- verified to exist and to define that function -- or a known gap carrying a reason and a reference. An entry with no anchors is NOT DETERMINED rather than a pass, because an entry that cannot describe the parity it asserts has not established one.

title: the io-row command applies each rotation flag to the axis the other one names
problem: The command that creates the four io rows takes a rotation flag per axis. Measured across a two-by-two of separate processes: the two horizontal rows follow the flag named for the vertical axis and are unmoved by the one named for their own, and the two vertical rows do the exact opposite. Each flag has a real, reproducible effect, so neither is ignored -- each acts on the axis the other names.
pattern: A tool accepts a per-axis flag and applies it to the other axis. Because both flags default to the identity rotation, every default run is correct and the crossing is invisible; the whole cost falls on the author who sets one deliberately, who then gets the rotation on the pair of sides they did not name. The tool's own help prints the flag names and no axis semantics, so nothing in the tool contradicts the reading its principal consumer publishes.
golden_sample: none -- there is no output in which the flags act on the axes they name, which is the finding. The expected behaviour is the one its consumer publishes: the consumer declares each variable as the rotation to apply to the sites of that axis, and passes each straight through to the matching flag.
tool_enhancement: In the io-row construction of the pad module, the per-axis rotation arguments reach the row builder crossed relative to the axis their flag names. Either exchange them at the call so each flag drives the rows it names, or -- if the naming follows an unstated convention where the word describes the orientation a placed cell takes rather than the axis of the row it sits in -- state that convention in the command help, where a caller reads it, since the consumer that ships with this tool documents the opposite. The same crossing is present in the site-selection flag pair of the same command and is established there without measuring an orientation at all, so whichever way it is resolved must be applied to both pairs together.
suggested_fix: Exchange the per-axis rotation and site arguments at the io-row construction call so each flag drives the axis it names, or document the opposite convention in the command help; the fix must cover both flag pairs together.
session_context: Found while converging a capture over another lane's pad-ring recovery. That lane swept four values of one rotation flag with the other held at the identity, concluded the variable was inert, and recorded a second observation -- that a pad on a horizontal side tracked the vertical flag -- as an oddity it did not chase. Those are one fact. A two-by-two varying both flags, one process per cell, resolves it, and a positive control at the site-selection flag pair of the same command reproduces the same crossing with no orientation reasoning involved.
why_not_bucket_a: The root cause is the tool's own argument routing. No plugin-side rule can put a rotation on the axis the caller named -- it can only decline to ask, which is the separate rule captured beside this record.

rule_name: a knob the flow cannot honour degrades loudly
pattern: A step declares a configuration variable, passes it to a tool, and the tool does not deliver what the variable's name promises. The step proceeds and reports a verdict. An author who sets the knob is told nothing: the run passes, the geometry is whatever the tool chose, and the setting that was supposed to control it changed nothing they can see. The failure is worst exactly where the author was most deliberate, and it is silent at every other setting because the default happens to be the identity.
docstring: Every variable in a step's declared contract is classified as honoured or not honoured, and the classification is a MEASUREMENT, not an assertion -- driven at the default and at one non-default value, comparing the observable result. A variable measured not honoured must degrade loudly in both directions: at the value indistinguishable from never having set it, PROCEED and record the finding in every report including the skipped ones, because a disclosure only on the happy path is not a disclosure; at a deliberately declared value, refuse NOT DETERMINED naming the variable. Never a pass, never a finding about the design -- I cannot honour what you asked is neither. Generalise the rule, never the one variable: what makes this a rule is that a knob an author can set and that changes nothing is a lie the flow tells, and nothing about that sentence mentions what the knob controls.
fix_action: NOT SHIPPED IN THIS BUNDLE, AND THE REASON IS NOT THAT IT NEEDS JUDGEMENT. The input is fully named: the step's declared variable contract, plus two runs of the step differing in one variable, plus the observable each run produces. The decision -- did the observable move -- is a comparison, with no judgement in it. What is missing is the SUBJECT: on this tree no step carries an honoured-versus-not-honoured classification at all, and the ruling that creates the first one is in an open, unlanded branch. A guard shipped tonight would therefore fire on the tree it shipped on, which is a bug and not a guard; and a guard narrowed until it stopped firing would be a guard that no longer asks the question. Land the ruling, then add the classification to the register that this bundle ships, then wire this check to drive the two runs and compare. The one thing that must not happen is the classification being written as a claim nobody measured, which is the same defect one layer up.

design: not a design finding — it was measured on this capture lane's own working tree
rule_name: a repair that cannot attribute a change has not attributed it
pattern: A gate drives other gates and tidies up after each one, restoring any tracked file that was clean before the drive and dirty after, on the reasoning that the child it just ran must have made the difference. Clean-before and dirty-after identifies a TIME WINDOW, not a writer. Anything else that writes inside that window matches the rule, and the restore command takes every uncommitted change in the file, because that command's meaning is make this equal the committed state and not undo the last write. The editor is told nothing: the work is gone, it was never committed, and the first sign of it is an unrelated failure later. And the lost work is the smaller half: because the repair attributes the change to whichever child happened to be running, the run also PUBLISHES A FINDING against that child — naming an innocent subject as having corrupted the checkout, in a list beside the real ones, where nothing distinguishes it.
docstring: A repair may undo only a change it can ATTRIBUTE. Timing is not attribution, and a docstring saying it is does not make it one. Where the writer cannot be established, the honest verdict is to NAME what changed and leave it, which is the rule this repository already applies to every other check that cannot answer its question. Three deterministic forms, any of which closes it: re-read the path immediately before restoring and refuse when it changed a second time inside one drive; make repair opt-in for a root the run does not own, since the argument that supplies that root is what takes it out of its designed setting; and in every case print the restored paths and the assumption behind the attribution, so an editor learns it from the gate and not from a later failure.
fix_action: NOT SHIPPED HERE, and the reason is scope and not difficulty. This was found while running the gate against the tree this lane was editing, it destroyed that work twice before it was identified, and a live positive control settles it: one line appended to a tracked file while the gate ran was gone twenty-six seconds later, silently. The evidence is in the bundle with the three fixes named. It is not patched here because the gate is shared, an instance was executing at the time, and a change to a restore path needs its own acceptance run rather than a same-night edit inside a brief about something else. It does NOT reproduce on a quiet tree, which is the setting it was designed for; it needs a second writer, which on a fleet where several agents share one repository is the normal condition.
